Your intuition is exactly right. When you hit YouTube's servers too hard, their anti-bot systems will flag your IP address and hit you with a 429 Too Many Requests error or a shadowban. The key to pulling a massive archive over a week or a month is flying under the radar by mimicking human pacing.

Here is the exact blueprint for running a "low and slow" extraction pipeline using yt-dlp without triggering alarms.

The Core Strategy

To avoid an IP ban, you need to randomize your request timings, throttle your bandwidth, and keep a strict ledger of what you've already grabbed so a failure doesn't force you to start over.

  1. Randomized Sleep Intervals: The biggest giveaway of an automated scraper is requesting a new video the exact millisecond the last one finishes.
  2. Bandwidth Throttling: Don't redline your connection. Downloading slower than the video's actual bitrate looks exactly like a human buffering a video while watching it.
  3. The Archive Ledger: This is mandatory for a job that spans weeks. It writes every successful download ID to a local text file. If the script crashes, you get rate-limited, or you need to restart a router, yt-dlp reads this file and skips previously downloaded videos entirely without making a single network request to YouTube.

The Configuration

Since you'll be running this continuously for weeks, the best approach is to drop this into a tmux session on your Mac Mini, detach, and just let it run in the background.

Here is the command structure to keep your IP safe:

yt-dlp \
  --limit-rate 2M \
  --sleep-interval 120 \
  --max-sleep-interval 400 \
  --sleep-subtitles 5 \
  --download-archive downloaded_ledger.txt \
  --ignore-errors \
  "YOUR_PLAYLIST_OR_CHANNEL_URL"

How the Math Works Out

Let's say you are pointing this at a channel with 1,000 videos.

SettingEffect
--limit-rate 2MCaps download speed at 2 Megabytes per second.
--sleep-interval 120Waits a minimum of 2 minutes between downloads.
--max-sleep-interval 400Waits a maximum of ~6.5 minutes between downloads.

With these settings, yt-dlp will wait a randomized average of 4.25 minutes between videos.

  • Daily Yield: ~330 videos per day.
  • Total Time for 1,000 Videos: ~3 days.

If you want to stretch that 1,000-video queue across a full month to be hyper-conservative, just bump the intervals up: --sleep-interval 900 (15 mins) and --max-sleep-interval 2700 (45 mins).

If You Do Get Flagged

If you push too hard and get slapped with a 429 error, it is almost always a soft, temporary block.

  • Kill the script immediately.
  • Wait 12 to 24 hours for the cooldown to expire.
  • When you fire the command back up, the --download-archive flag ensures it picks up exactly where it left off without re-triggering the ban by checking older videos.

You are completely right to think about the macro-level pacing. While randomized seconds between downloads help, algorithms look for patterns over days. A script that runs 24/7, even with randomized delays, eventually looks synthetic. Breaking it up into daily chunks with massive "cooling off" periods is the safest approach.

Here is how we address all three of your requirements: the 1080p cap, the failure retries, and the batching schedule.

1. Capping at 1080p

By default, yt-dlp tries to pull the highest possible resolution, which means massive 4K WebM files. To force it to grab the best quality up to 1080p (and preferably in an easy-to-use format like MP4), you need a specific format filter.

We will use this flag: -f "bestvideo[height<=1080][ext=mp4]+bestaudio[ext=m4a]/best[height<=1080]/best"

This tells the tool: "Find the best video stream that is 1080p or smaller, merge it with the best audio, and if you can't find that exact combination, just give me the best pre-merged 1080p file you have."

2. How the Archive Handles Failures

You don't need to do anything special to retry failed downloads. The --download-archive flag is incredibly strict: it only writes a video ID to your ledger file after the file has completely and successfully downloaded and merged on your hard drive.

If your internet drops, the video gets corrupted, or YouTube blocks the request halfway through, that ID never gets written. The next time the script runs, it will see the video is missing from the ledger and automatically try downloading it again.

3. The "Half-Day Off" Pacing Script

Since yt-dlp doesn't have a built-in "take a 12-hour nap" command, we can wrap it in a simple loop using your Fish shell. yt-dlp has a --max-downloads flag, which makes this incredibly easy.

Here is a Fish script you can run. It tells yt-dlp to download a small batch, stop, and then tells your terminal to sleep for 12 hours before starting the next batch.

while true
    echo "Starting a new extraction batch..."
    
    yt-dlp \
        -f "bestvideo[height<=1080][ext=mp4]+bestaudio[ext=m4a]/best[height<=1080]/best" \
        --download-archive completed_ledger.txt \
        --sleep-interval 120 \
        --max-sleep-interval 400 \
        --max-downloads 25 \
        --ignore-errors \
        "YOUR_PLAYLIST_OR_CHANNEL_URL"
        
    echo "Batch complete. Sleeping for 12 hours to relax the buffer..."
    # Sleep takes seconds. 12 hours = 43200 seconds.
    sleep 43200
end

How this specific loop behaves:

  1. It starts up and checks completed_ledger.txt to instantly skip everything you already have.
  2. It downloads up to 25 new videos, pausing for 2 to 6 minutes between each one.
  3. Once it hits exactly 25 successful downloads, yt-dlp shuts down.
  4. The Fish loop takes over, waits exactly 12 hours, and then triggers step 1 all over again.

You can drop this right into your terminal and let it slowly chip away at massive channels completely unattended.

Decoupling the playlist extraction from the actual downloading is the perfect way to build a deterministic, forecastable schedule.

To do this, we break the process into two phases: a high-speed metadata scrape to get the list of URLs, followed by an execution script that shuffles the list, pre-calculates every single sleep interval, and outputs a highly accurate ETA before downloading a single byte.

Since you need to calculate times, track batches, and manage execution state, Python is the best tool to orchestrate yt-dlp here.

The Orchestration Script

This Python script uses yt-dlp to fetch the video IDs silently, builds your randomized schedule, calculates the exact time footprint (including 12-hour batch rests), and then executes the downloads one by one.

Save this as download_orchestrator.py and run it from your terminal:

import subprocess
import random
import time
from datetime import timedelta

# --- Configuration ---
URL = "YOUR_PLAYLIST_OR_CHANNEL_URL"
BATCH_SIZE = 25
MIN_SLEEP = 120      # 2 minutes
MAX_SLEEP = 400      # ~6.5 minutes
HALF_DAY_REST = 43200 # 12 hours

def get_video_ids(url):
    print("Fetching video list from YouTube (metadata only)...")
    # --flat-playlist prevents downloading; --print id just outputs the video IDs
    raw_output = subprocess.check_output(
        ["yt-dlp", "--flat-playlist", "--print", "id", url], 
        text=True
    )
    return [vid.strip() for vid in raw_output.strip().split('\n') if vid.strip()]

def main():
    video_ids = get_video_ids(URL)
    
    # Randomize the sequence upfront
    random.shuffle(video_ids)
    total_videos = len(video_ids)
    print(f"Found {total_videos} videos. Generating schedule...\n")

    total_sleep_seconds = 0
    schedule = []

    # Pre-bake the timers and batches
    for i, vid in enumerate(video_ids):
        sleep_time = random.randint(MIN_SLEEP, MAX_SLEEP)
        is_batch_end = (i + 1) % BATCH_SIZE == 0
        
        schedule.append((vid, sleep_time, is_batch_end))
        
        # Add to total time forecast (don't add sleep after the very last video)
        if i != total_videos - 1:
            total_sleep_seconds += sleep_time
            if is_batch_end:
                total_sleep_seconds += HALF_DAY_REST

    # Add an estimated 2.5 minutes per video for the actual download time 
    # to make the forecast highly accurate.
    estimated_download_time = total_videos * 150 
    total_eta = total_sleep_seconds + estimated_download_time

    print(f"--- FORECAST ---")
    print(f"Total Videos: {total_videos}")
    print(f"Estimated Completion Time: {timedelta(seconds=total_eta)}")
    print(f"----------------\n")
    
    time.sleep(3) # Give you a moment to read the ETA before it starts

    # Execute the schedule
    for i, (vid, sleep_time, is_batch_end) in enumerate(schedule):
        print(f"[{i+1}/{total_videos}] Initiating download for {vid}...")
        
        # Let yt-dlp handle the actual 1080p download and ledger checking
        subprocess.run([
            "yt-dlp",
            "-f", "bestvideo[height<=1080][ext=mp4]+bestaudio[ext=m4a]/best[height<=1080]/best",
            "--download-archive", "completed_ledger.txt",
            "--ignore-errors",
            f"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v={vid}"
        ])
        
        if i == total_videos - 1:
            print("Archive complete.")
            break
            
        if is_batch_end:
            print(f"Batch limit reached. Relaxing buffer for 12 hours...")
            time.sleep(HALF_DAY_REST)
        else:
            print(f"Sleeping for {sleep_time} seconds before next request...")
            time.sleep(sleep_time)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

How This Pipeline Behaves

  1. Phase 1: Fast Scrape: The --flat-playlist command pulls just the IDs. This takes a few seconds even for a massive channel, meaning you don't trigger any rate limits just mapping out the territory.
  2. Phase 2: Forecasting: Python shuffles the IDs, loops through them to assign a random integer for the sleep interval, and injects the 12-hour penalty every 25th video. It sums this all up using datetime.timedelta so you get a clean readout like Estimated Completion Time: 14 days, 6:15:30.
  3. Phase 3: Execution: It hands the video ID off to yt-dlp one at a time. yt-dlp immediately checks completed_ledger.txt. If the video is already there, yt-dlp exits instantly, and Python moves on to the next sleep timer.

If the script crashes or you manually stop it: When you restart it, Python will fetch the playlist again and generate a brand new random sequence. Because yt-dlp checks the ledger, it will instantly skip the ones you already grabbed and naturally resume chipping away at the remaining videos in a completely fresh order — which actually makes your traffic look even more randomized to YouTube's detection systems.

  3. Phase 3: Execution & State Management
